doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

title: The baton-throwing conductor and alternate fingerings
summary: On a TV movie Shew cannot double-tongue a page, a conductor throws a baton, and he solves it with Kenny Dorham's alternate fingerings.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: things. Sometimes, and I got caught one time on a film, a TV movie about some inconsequential invasion of bees in an Indiana small village. Who knew? It was not important but there was only one trumpet on the thing and I turned the page and there was a whole bunch of double tonguing. And I tried to do it and I really couldn’t do it. I could not handle it. And I went oh, and you’ve got 30 seconds to get it ready. And so I did it one time and it was terrible. And the conductor goes, “Take two.” Oh you want to hear that again? So I’m going, oh crap. So I couldn’t do it. And he stopped and he looked at me and he said, “Is there a problem, sir?” And I said, me and my big mouth I had to say, “Man it’s not my bag you dig?” and he threw the baton at me. And this was in front of like an 80 piece orchestra and I’m the only trumpet. And the contractor was Gus Klein who was Manny Klein’s son. You know? And Gus is a good guy but Gus leans over and he says, “Bobby, what the hell are you doing?” I said, “What are you doing putting me on a session like this?” But he doesn’t know, the contractor doesn’t know what the music is. He just gets a call from the writer and he’s not looking at the parts. He doesn’t go through everybody’s part and says oh we can’t hire Bobby for this there’s double tonguing on one page you know. So they hire you and you’re expected to be able to be the most eclectic guy on the planet. You’ve got to walk in there and do everything. So what happened is I had to go out and talk to the guy and apologize and everything. And I said, “Look, I’m sorry, I don’t mean to be — but it intimidated me when you throw a baton at me it doesn’t make it easier.” I says, “I’ll go in there now and I’ll figure out how to play this thing for you but if it requires that I pay for the entire orchestra for an extra hour I will pay it, ten thousand dollars, but I’m not going to take a baton in the face. Money is not that important to me, if that’s what it’s going to take.” So I walked in there and I sat down and everybody was looking at me like ooh. And I walked over there and I looked at that thing and I thought how in the hell am I going to do this? And then I remembered when I got out of high school I went back to New York and I used to go out and listen to Kenny Dorham and Roy Eldridge and all these guys play. And they used to do, I used to watch Kenny Dorham and he used to do a thing with alternate fingerings. And he’d do things like this [plays his trumpet]. And I went damn, how’s he do that? And I messed around and I went alternate fingerings. So I went in there and I put a mute in and I practiced this page using alternate fingerings until I could do it. And the guy came in and he looked at me and he said, “Are we ready?” And I went, “Yes sir, we are.” And everybody in the orchestra went what? He learned to double tongue that fast you know? And I did it and the guy thought I double tongued it. He never knew that I was only using alternate fingerings like that. And on the trumpet there’s a lot of ‘em. And if you know ‘em you can bullshit your way right through it. And I walked out of that studio that day like whew, oh God.

Well you kind of said it earlier in the interview that you’ve got to keep your wits about you. And you know if you had like freaked out you probably wouldn’t have had that memory of seeing those guys do that alternate fingering.
